Some words on co-op:

There's been a lot of talk about how Star Wars Battlefront is a "couch co-op game." And that's not entirely inaccurate. There is a co-op mode where you and a pal play as rebels, fighting off hordes of troopers and some AT-STs in a survival mode. We've written about it before. On consoles, it's a "couch co-op" game, since you can play it splitscreen with a buddy. The PC version doesn't have splitscreen, so unless you both happen to have your PC's on a table in front of your couch (which, seems less than comfortable, but possible) it's just straight up co-op.

That being said, the vast majority of the game isn't co-op. It's versus. Even if you and a handful of friends join forces, you're still waging war against another handful of human beings. We here at Co-Optimus hold the definition of co-op to be:

"A co-op game is a game where two or more players work together to accomplish a goal against AI opponents."

We're still showcasing Star Wars Battlefront, because the "Survival Mode" does look like a ton of fun. It might not be the main feature of the game, but I'm certain at least of few of us will bank a few hours into it. For that reason, we're looking forward to November 17th.

Summary: I am proposing a new system of video game reviews, that will both add transparency to the reviews, filter out the shills, and make consumer written reviews more accurate.

Years ago, there was a magazine called EGM, and they had the best video game review system ever.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Gaming_Monthly From the wikipedia article

Games are reviewed by one member (originally a team of four until the year 2000, then a team of three, and finally knocked down to one in 2008), except for "the big games", which were reviewed by one of a pool of editors known as "The Review Crew." They each assign a grade to the game and write a few paragraphs about their opinion of the game.

The way the system worked, was that each reviewer had a biography. this told you what their interests where, and if they had similar interests to you, then you would either like the game, or hate it based on their reviews. I found that this was both the most accurate system, as well as the fairest. It also made for some interesting reading.

But how does this affect us? Its simple, from now on, when we write a meta critic review, or a steam review, we list our three most played games, or our three recent favorites, and then we write our review.

So if you like sand box games, then write a review of a sand box, then other people who also like sand box games will take your review more seriously. the same is true if you do not play a lot of sand box games, but still review a sandbox you bought. Regardless of what you like or play the most of, your taste preferences will help other consumers judge the game in a more realistic way.

This is important. It has occurred to me, that many of these reviewers for the big publications, do not play as much games as everyone else does. this makes me wonder how they are qualified to review a game?

Just adding our three top games to our written reviews, will go a long way towards making the game journos forgotten. The best part, is not everyone has to do it, just enough people, and you do not have to be in gg to do this. So there is a good chance that this will catch on with everyone else too.
